title: Plants in Bhartiya Gyan Parampara
sub: Botany, history of botany in India, Vedic concepts, Indian Rishis and traditional plant knowledge.
topics: Botany — Definition, Scope and Importance
Plant science and its major branches

Definition: Botany is the branch of Biology dealing with the scientific study of plants, including their structure, growth, reproduction, metabolism, diseases and evolutionary relationships. It is also called Plant Biology or Phytology.

Major branches

  • Morphology — external form
  • Anatomy — internal structure
  • Physiology — life functions
  • Taxonomy — classification and naming
  • Ecology — plants and environment

Importance

  • Food and oxygen supply
  • Plant-derived medicines
  • Timber, rubber, cotton and spices
  • Soil and climate regulation
  • Research and biofuel development
Diagram: branches of Botany / importance of plants.
History of Botany in India
Ancient to modern development

Ancient and Medieval

Rigveda and Atharvaveda described plants; Parashar's Vrikshayurveda and the Charaka and Sushruta traditions contributed to plant knowledge. Mughal-period gardens and horticulture expanded plant use and cultivation.

British and Modern

William Roxburgh is described as the Father of Indian Botany and J.D. Hooker compiled Flora of British India. Modern development includes the Botanical Survey of India, CSIR/ICAR research, Green Revolution work and J.C. Bose's studies of plant sensitivity.
Timeline: Ancient → Medieval → British → Modern.
Botanical Concepts in Vedas, Upanishads, Ramayan and Puranas
Traditional classification and plant knowledge

Vedic concepts

Rigveda: Vanaspati, Vriksha, Oshadhi and Virudh. Atharvaveda contains extensive references to medicinal plants and the concept of Bheshaj.

Later texts

Upanishads discuss plant consciousness. Ramayan mentions Ashoka Vatika, Panchavati and Sanjeevani. Puranic texts describe plant categories and medicinal or sacred plants.

title: Morphology — External Structure of Plants
sub: Thallus and cormus, modifications of roots, stems and leaves, and reproductive external structures.
topics: Basic Concepts — Thallus vs Plant Body
Lower plant body and differentiated cormus

Thallus

Body undivided; root, stem and leaf differentiation absent; vascular tissue absent. Examples include Spirogyra, Ulva and Marchantia.

Plant Body (Cormus)

Root, stem and leaf are distinct; vascular tissue is present. Seen in ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms.

title: Anatomy — Internal Structure of Plants
sub: Plant cell, tissues and comparative anatomy of roots, stems and leaves.
topics: Plant Cell — Structure
Cell theory and major organelles

Cell Theory: Schleiden (1838), Schwann (1839) and Virchow (1855): “Omnis cellula e cellula”.

Plant-specific prominence

Cell wall provides support; chloroplast performs photosynthesis and has its own DNA; the large vacuole maintains turgor and stores materials.

Other organelles

Plasma membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, Golgi apparatus and rough/smooth ER perform transport, control, respiration, protein synthesis and packaging functions.
Labelled plant cell.
Tissues — Classification
Meristematic and permanent tissues

Meristematic

  • Apical — primary growth
  • Lateral — secondary growth
  • Intercalary — internode growth

Permanent

  • Parenchyma — storage/photosynthesis
  • Collenchyma — flexible support
  • Sclerenchyma — rigid support
  • Xylem — water/mineral conduction
  • Phloem — food conduction
Tissue classification chart.
Dicot and Monocot Root Anatomy
Internal comparison

Dicot root

Radial bundles, fewer xylem arms, cambium associated with secondary growth and pith small or absent.

Monocot root

Radial polyarch bundles, large distinct pith and no secondary growth.
Cross-section: dicot root vs monocot root.
Dicot and Monocot Stem Anatomy
Vascular arrangement and secondary growth

Dicot stem

Collenchymatous hypodermis; vascular bundles in a ring, open and collateral; secondary growth possible.

Monocot stem

Sclerenchymatous hypodermis; vascular bundles scattered, closed and collateral; secondary growth absent.
Cross-section: dicot stem vs monocot stem.
Leaf Anatomy
Dorsiventral and isobilateral leaf structure

Dorsiventral (dicot)

Upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll and lower epidermis with abundant stomata.

Isobilateral (monocot)

Stomata on both epidermal surfaces; mesophyll generally undifferentiated; Kranz anatomy and bulliform cells are important features in the source notes.

title: General Idea of Plant Physiology
sub: Water relations, transpiration, ascent of sap, photosynthesis and respiration.
topics: Water Relations
Diffusion, osmosis, imbibition and water potential

Water potential: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp. Pure water has Ψ = 0; solutes make water potential negative.

Key processes

  • Diffusion — high to low concentration
  • Osmosis — water through a semipermeable membrane
  • Imbibition — water absorption by solid colloids

Cell states

  • Turgidity — fully hydrated, maximum turgor
  • Plasmolysis — membrane shrinks away from wall in hypertonic solution
  • Deplasmolysis can reverse plasmolysis
Water movement / plasmolysis diagram.
Transpiration and Ascent of Sap
Water loss and cohesion-tension mechanism

Transpiration types

Stomatal: 80–90%; Cuticular: 10–20%; Lenticular: less than 1% in the source notes.

Cohesion-Tension Theory

Dixon and Joly (1894): transpiration creates tension in xylem; cohesion and adhesion maintain a continuous water column from roots to leaves.
Ascent of sap through xylem.
Photosynthesis
Light reactions, Calvin cycle, C4 and CAM

Overall equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, requiring light and chlorophyll.

Light and C3 reactions

Light reactions occur in thylakoid membranes and form ATP/NADPH with O₂ release. The Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma and fixes CO₂ through RuBP/Rubisco.

C4 and CAM

C4 plants use mesophyll and bundle sheath with OAA as first product. CAM plants open stomata mainly at night and store CO₂ as malic acid.
Chloroplast with grana and stroma; pathway flow.
Respiration
Glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, Krebs cycle and ETC

Equation in source notes: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + 38 ATP.

Stages

  • Glycolysis — cytoplasm; net 2 ATP
  • Pyruvate oxidation — mitochondrial matrix
  • Krebs cycle — matrix; 2 ATP

ETC and RQ

Oxidative phosphorylation occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane and is listed as 32–34 ATP. RQ = CO₂ released / O₂ absorbed.
Mitochondrion and respiration stages.
Physiology Integration
Linking water, transport, photosynthesis and respiration

Core revision logic

Water enters and moves through the plant; transpiration drives the water column; photosynthesis captures energy and forms carbohydrates; respiration releases usable energy as ATP.

title: Plant Reproduction, Growth and Propagation
sub: Propagules, sexual and asexual reproduction, hormones, elicitors and alternation of generations.
topics: Plant Propagation — Types of Propagules
Natural and artificial propagation

Natural propagules

Rhizome, tuber, bulb, corm, runner, sucker, bulbil and foliar buds are listed with examples such as ginger, potato, onion, banana, Agave and Bryophyllum.

Artificial methods

Cutting uses a stem/leaf/root piece; grafting joins stock and scion. Examples in the source include rose, hibiscus, begonia, mango and apple.
Vegetative propagation examples.
Sexual and Asexual Reproduction
Double fertilization and pollination

Double fertilization: Sperm + egg → zygote (2n) → embryo; second sperm + two polar nuclei → endosperm (3n). The source notes identify this as unique to angiosperms and credit Nawaschin (1898).

Pollination

  • Autogamy — self
  • Anemophily — wind
  • Entomophily — insects

More agents

  • Hydrophily — water
  • Ornithophily — birds
Double fertilization and pollination types.
Plant Hormones and Role of Elicitors
Growth regulators and defence signalling

Hormones

  • Auxin — elongation, rooting, apical dominance
  • Gibberellin — elongation, germination, bolting
  • Cytokinin — cell division, shoot differentiation
  • ABA — dormancy and stomatal closure
  • Ethylene — ripening and senescence

Elicitors

Biotic or abiotic signals such as pathogen factors, UV, heat or wounding can trigger defence, secondary metabolites and systemic acquired resistance (SAR).

Gametophyte and Sporophyte
Dominant phases in major plant groups

Groups

Algae and bryophytes have a prominent gametophyte phase in the source table, while pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms are described with dominant sporophytes.

Reduction of gametophyte

In seed plants the gametophytes are highly reduced, represented by structures such as pollen and embryo sac.
Compare dominant phase across plant groups.
Alternation of Generations
Cycle between haploid and diploid phases

Cycle: Sporophyte (2n) → meiosis → spores (n) → mitosis → gametophyte (n) → gametes and fertilization → zygote (2n) → new sporophyte.

Remember

Meiosis produces spores and reduces chromosome number; mitosis develops the gametophyte; fertilization restores the diploid sporophyte generation.
